title: Reminder – pituitary physiology
html:
Source: REMINDER Physio 2nd year- Pituitary gland.pdf – 15 pages

PITUITARY GLAND (HYPOPHYSIS) #1

  • -small endocrine gland (10/12/6 mm)
  • -weight: 0.5 g
  • -localized -in a small bony cavity (hypophyseal fossa in sella turcica of sphenoid
  • bone), at the brain base, in front of hypothalamus
  • -is connected to hypothalamus through infundibulum
  • -infundibulum -contains nervous fibres and small blood vessels
  • -has 2 parts (anatomically and physiologically distinct):
  • -anterior lobe (adenohypophysis)
  • -results from Rathke’s pouch (epithelial tissue), that
  • migrates upward from the embryonic mouth,
  • to an adjacent position of neural tissue
  • that comes downward from diencephalon (this part,
  • in contact with neurohypophysis forms
  • intermedia lobe)
  • -is connected to hypothalamus through vessels
  • - posterior lobe -derives from brain
  • -is formed by nervous tissue = neurohypophysis
  • -is connected to hypothalamus through neural tract
  • -adenohypophysis hormones -act on different target organs
  • => hypophysis gland = the main endocrine gland

ANTERIOR PITUITARY #2

  • -pars distalis = anterior pituitary
  • -pars intermedia -between the anterior and posterior parts of the pituitary
  • -pars tuberalis = the thin extension in contact with the infundibulum
  • -origin -glandular (adeno = glandular)
  • Structure
  • -contains glandular cells -contains granules with hormones
  • -arranged in clusters, surrounded by capillary network
  • Secretion
  • -adenohypophysis -secretes 6 hormones, as a result of the signals transmitted from
  • hypothalamus through the hypothalamo-hypophyseal portal system

HYPOTHALAMO-ADENOHYPOPHYSEAL COMMUNICATION #3

  • -the hypothalamic regulatory factors come to the adenohypophysis cells through 2
  • capillary plexuses
  • -superior hypophyseal arterial system -2 origins -internal carotid artery
  • -posterior communicant arteries
  • from Willis polygon
  • -is a short arterial system that immediately
  • branches, leading to primary plexus
  • -Primary capillary plexus -placed at the anterior part of the hypothalamus
  • -made of sinusoidal capillaries
  • -confluence into hypophyseal portal veins that transports
  • the blood through infundibulum to the anterior pituitary
  • -Secondary capillary plexus -the vessels of the hypophyseal portal veins branch out
  • again
  • -drain into anterior hypophyseal veins, from where the
  • hormones are transported to the target organs

-hypothalamo-hypophyseal portal system: #4

  • -made the nervous and vascular communications between:
  • hypothalamus
  • adenohypophysis
  • -facilitates the signals’ transmission from the CNS to adenohypophysis
  • -because of the fenestrated capillaries, the hormonal molecules can be
  • transported between hypothalamus and hypophysis
  • Adenohypophysis Control
  • -releasing or inhibiting hormones
  • -regulate synthesis and secretion of adenohypophysis hormones
  • -are produced in hypothalamus
  • -are transported through the hypothalamo-hypophyseal portal system into the
  • anterior pituitary, in the proximity of the hormone-producing cells
  • -the main factors that regulate adenohypophysis functions are:
  • -CRH = corticotropin-releasing hormone
  • -TRH = thyrotropin-releasing hormone
  • -GnRH = gonadotropin-releasing hormone
  • -GHRH = growth hormone-releasing hormone
  • -GIH = somatostatin = inhibitor of growth hormone secretion
  • -PRF = prolactin-releasing factor
  • -PIF = prolactin-inhibitory factor

Feedback Regulation of the Hypothalamo-Hypophyseal System #5

  • -3 types of feedback systems:
  • 1. Long loop system
  • Hypothalamus
  • Adenohypophysis’ act on target organ hormone synthesis
  • hormones (ex. suprarenal gland) (cortisol)
  • the secreted hormone regulates through negative feedback the
  • hypothalamus and adenohypophysis
  • 2. Short loop system
  • Hypothalamus Adenohypophysis hormone
  • adenohypophysis hormone acts on
  • hypothalamus through negative feedback
  • 3. Ultrashort loop system
  • Hypothalamus hypophysotroph regulator hypophysis
  • the regulator hormone acts directly
  • on hypothalamus to control its own secretion

Pulsatile Secretion of Hypothalamic and Hypophyseal Hormones #6

  • Pulsatile episodic secretion
  • = releasing of the hormones, regularly and for a short time
  • -imposed by longer rhythms (diurnal, seasonal)
  • -is a function of the intrinsic nervous oscillators located inside the hormone-
  • producing cells
  • Adenohypophysis Hormones
  • 1. Luteinizing Hormone(LH)
  • -target cells -in female -ovary
  • -in male -Leydig cells
  • LH -in female -stimulates ovulation and the conversion of the ovulated ovarian
  • follicle into an endocrine structure: corpus luteum
  • -stimulates estrogens and progesterone secretion
  • -the high concentration of LH during the 14th day of the ovarian cycle
  • represents the pro-ovulatory stimulus
  • -in male -is the main regulator of the steroid synthesis in the testis
  • -LH (= interstitial cell-stimulating hormone = ICSH) stimulates:
  • -the cells of Leydig to produce androgens
  • -the testis growth
  • -anabolic steroids used in body building -block the LH secretion and
  • determine testis atrophy
  • -LH and FSH are secreted by the same cell = gonadotropine cell
  • -LH and FSH secretion is regulated by gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH),
  • hormone secreted by the hypothalamus
  • -dopamine, endorphins and melatonin -inhibit GnRH secretion
  • -noradrenalin -stimulates GnRH secretion

2. Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) #7

  • -in female -act on the ovarian follicle
  • -stimulates the growth of the granulosa cells
  • -stimulates the transformation of the androgens into estrogens (in the
  • theca cells)
  • -in male -acts on Sertoli cells
  • -stimulates estrogens synthesis from androgens
  • -stimulates production of the protein that bind the androgen (higher
  • concentration of androgens is maintained in the proximity of the cells that
  • produce spermatozoa
  • 3. Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH)
  • -regulates the growth and the metabolism of the thyroid gland
  • -stimulates synthesis and secretion of thyroid hormones
  • -thyroid-releasing hormone (TRH) -produced in hypothalamus
  • -stimulates TSH secretion
  • 4. Pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC)
  • = pre-pro-hormone
  • -is the precursor for ACTH and for beta-lipotropin (β-LPH)
  • 5. Adrenocorticotropic hormone(ACTH)
  • -stimulates the steroids synthesis in the adrenal cortex
  • Secretion control
  • - ACTH secretion can be modified by numerous factors:
  • -corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH)
  • -secreted in the hypothalamus (pulsatile secretion)
  • -increases the ACTH synthesis

-ACTH secretion -has rhythmical diurnal variations, according to different types of #8

  • stress
  • -maximum -in the morning
  • -minimum –in the evening
  • -factors that stimulate ACTH secretion:
  • - stress (operation, trauma, infections, hypoxia)
  • - acute hypoglycaemia
  • - hypoxia
  • - anxiety, depression
  • - α- and β-adrenergic agonists
  • -factors that inhibit ACTH secretion:
  • -cortisol -has a negative-feedback effect on -hypophysis -blocks the ACTH
  • synthesis and secretion
  • -hypothalamus -decreases the
  • release of CRH
  • 6. Growth hormone(STH, somatotropin)
  • -STH secretion -pulsatile (diurnal rhythm)
  • -maximum -early morning, just before wakening
  • -secretion is stimulated during profound sleep
  • -STH -stimulates body growth and has metabolic actions
  • Metabolic actions
  • 1. Carbohydrates metabolism - glycaemia (STH decreases glucose degradation
  • in the skeletal muscle and adipose tissue)
  • - the peripheral sensitivity to insulin (STH is
  • considered a hormone that can lead to diabetes)
  • - hepatic production of glucose
  • -STH- is necessary for insulin secretion

2.Protein metabolism - amino acids capture inside the cells #9

  • - protein synthesis from amino acids
  • - urea production
  • -produces nitrogen retention
  • 3. Lipid metabolism lipolysis
  • synthesis of ketone bodies
  • Actions on growth
  • -STH -stimulates the growth of the skelton and of the viscera
  • -in children-the absence of STH leads to pituitary dwarfism
  • -excessive STH secretion -during childhood -develops gigantism
  • -after puberty -leads to acromegaly (Greek: akron = top,
  • megas = large)
  • Insulin-Like Growth Factors
  • -regulate cell proliferation, differentiation and the cellular metabolism
  • -regulate the STH action on cartilage and the bone growth
  • -IGF-I -is produced in almost all adult tissues
  • -IGF-II -is produced in embryo
  • -stimulate -the DNA synthesis and protein synthesis
  • -growth of bones, cartilages, soft tissues

STH and IGF-1 negative feedback loops: #10

  • STH stimulates secretion of IGF-1 from peripheral target tissue
  • IGF-1 then -directly -inhibits STH release by suppressing the somatotrophs
  • -indirectly -inhibits STH release by suppressing GHRH release
  • from the arcuate nucleus in hypothalamus
  • -indirectly -inhibits STH release by increasing secretion of
  • somatostatin from nuclei in the periventricular region
  • STH -inhibits its own secretion via „short loop” feedback on somatotrophs
  • Control of STH release
  • -hypothalamus -releases -somatostatin (GIH, growth –inhibiting hormone)
  • -growth-releasing hormone (GRH)
  • -hypoglycaemia
  • -profound sleep
  • -stress STH secretion
  • -physical effort
  • 7. Prolactin (PRL)
  • -in male and female –has similar basal seric concentrations of PRL
  • Actions:
  • 1. initiation and maintaining the lactation
  • Mammogenic effect = promotion of the mammary growth under the action of
  • many hormones
  • -estrogens and progesterone -are the first hormones implicated
  • Lactogenic effect = initiation of milk secretion
  • -pregnancy -estrogens, progesterone, hPL (human placental lactogens),
  • STH, insulin, cortisol, and thyroid hormones promote the
  • development of mammary glands
  • -milk production -is inhibited by high levels of estrogens
  • and progesterone

-at birth - estrogens and progesterone permit the PRL to #11

  • stimulate lactation
  • - cortisol facilitates initiation (but not the
  • maintenance) of lactation
  • -estradiol -antagonist for PRL
  • -can stop lactation
  • Galactopoietic effect = the maintenance of milk production once it has been
  • established
  • -it requires PRL and oxytocin
  • 2. The excessive secretion of PRL inhibits the reproductive function in both male and
  • female
  • Control of prolactin release
  • Stimuli that lead to prolactin release:
  • -the birth
  • -mammary gland stimulation -in non-pregnant woman
  • -during menstruation -minimum response
  • -in man- no response
  • -stress
  • -physical effort
  • -sleep
  • -estrogens
  • -medicaments that interfere with dopamine synthesis
  • Substances that inhibit PRL secretion -dopamine
  • -dopamine agonists
  • -somatostatin

PARS INTERMEDIA #12

  • -produces different forms of melanocyte-stimulating hormone (MSH)
  • -in lower vertebrates (fish, amphibians, and reptiles) cause a darkening of the
  • skin to provide camouflage
  • -exogenous administration of MSH to humans stimulates melanin (pigment)
  • production in the melanocytes of skin
  • -produces -beta-endorphin (with opioid action in the CNS)
  • -gamma-lipotropin = γ-LPH (a lipolitic substance)
  • POSTERIOR PITUITARY
  • -does not act as an endocrine gland
  • -stores the hormones that are synthesised in hypothalamus
  • -specific cells -synthesise the inactive pro-hormone that is transported
  • through the hypothalamo-hypophyseal tract
  • (secretory granules)
  • -during transport -the pro-hormone release the active hormone, that is
  • stored in the posterior pituitary
  • -the hypothalamo-hypophyseal tract -transmits electric impulses that release
  • hormones into the blood
  • -the hormones: ADH, oxytocin

Antidiuretic hormone (ADH) #13

  • Renal actions
  • -increases the permeability for H O in the collecting ducts (nephron)
  • -ADH AMPc activates protein-kinases that phosphorilate
  • the proteins from the lumen membrane structure is rearranged
  • microtubules, microfilaments
  • = > permeability for water, urea and other dissolved substances
  • = > urinary volume
  • urine osmolarity
  • -ADH intensifies the contraction of the mesangial cells
  • => glomerular filtration ( => urinary volume decreases again)
  • -ADH -inhibits the renin release
  • Cardiovascular actions
  • -physiologically -ADH -does not modify the vascular tonus
  • -ADH -in high concentrations -has powerful pressing effects on vessels
  • (= vasopressin)
  • -acts directly on the arteriolar smooth muscle
  • -ADH -can increase arterial pressure with 35-50 mm Hg after acute haemorrhage
  • -in some types of vascular hypertension -scientists assume that ADH interacts with
  • the vessels’ smooth muscle, that becomes hyper-reactive to ADH

Actions on hypothalamo- hypophysio-corticosuprarenal axis #14

  • -ADH -stimulates ACTH secretions (directly and indirectly)
  • -is released in stress -by activation of the hypothalamo- hypophysio-
  • corticosuprarenal axis
  • Control of ADH secretion:
  • 1. osmolarity of the extracellular fluid
  • -increases of the extracellular fluid osmolarity determine the water to pass out of the
  • osmoreceptor cells cellular dehydration (=stimulus for osmoreceptor)
  • increases of the action potentials in the hypothalamo-hypophyseal tract
  • ADH release in the posterior pituitary
  • -if the serumal osmolarity increases with minimum 1%, the increase of ADH
  • concentration can be measured
  • -the primordial regulators are the volume receptors in the atria
  • 2. Alcohol -efficient suppressor of ADH secretion dehydration
  • Thirst –regulates the oral intake of water
  • -increased serumal osmolarity
  • -decreased vascular volume stimuli for thirst sensation
  • -ADH secretion
  • Oxytocin
  • Uterus motility
  • -oxytocin stimulates the contraction of the uterus
  • -estrogens - the uterus response to oxytocin
  • -progesterone - the uterus response to oxytocin
  • -oxytocin secretion increases only after the labour starts (birth)
  • (it is not a factor that initiates the birth)

-the stretch of cervix stimulates the receptors for distension and transmits afferent #15

  • impulses to the hypothalamus
  • => action potentials that release oxytocin (positive feedback)
  • uterine contraction
  • -sex act -can stimulate the oxytocin release in both male and female
  • -in male -the oxytocin role is unknown
  • -in female -it stimulates the uterine motility that facilitates the
  • sperm transport inside the reproductive female tract
  • Milk ejection
  • -oxytocin -stimulates the contraction of the myoepithelial cells that are arranged
  • longitudinally on the lactiferous ducts and around the alveoli in the breast
  • milk is pushed from the profoundness of the gland into the
  • larger ducts from where the new-born can suck it
  • = milk ejection
  • -oxytocin release is controlled by a neuro-humoral reflex:
  • -suckling or tactile stimulation -activate the local sensory receptors localized in
  • the nipple
  • -the sensory fibres transmit impulses to the hypothalamus
  • Other actions
  • - stimulates Na+ retention and anti-diuresis
  • - stimulates the contraction of smooth muscle in some viscera
  • - produces vasodilation that decreases the systolic arterial blood pressure
  • (especially cutaneous vasodilation)
  • - increases the prolactin concentration in plasma
  • - stimulates the spermatozoa elimination in the seminal ducts
